# Dissent is the data you are throwing away

Source: https://lowob.com/research/dissent-is-the-data-you-are-throwing-away/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-10 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When a committee decides, the minority view is smoothed out of the record. Over time, recorded dissent is often the most predictive signal an organisation has, and it costs one line to keep. Four decades of group research explain why it disappears: discussion favours what everyone already knows, members follow the most senior voice, and role-played objections carry less weight than real ones. Capture views before discussion, attribute them, attach a probability, and check them against outcomes.

## Key points

- In Stasser and Titus's classic 1985 experiment, group discussion "tended to perpetuate, not to correct" members' biased views, because information only some members held was rarely raised.
- Sunstein and Hastie advise leaders to consider staying silent, because groups follow their most senior, most talkative members.
- Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein's "decision hygiene" includes aggregating independent judgments, which only works if views are collected before they converge.
- Charlan Nemeth's research finds an assigned devil's advocate stimulates less thinking than genuine dissent.
- Edmondson's study of 51 work teams linked psychological safety to learning behaviour, so a dissent record must make disagreement safer, not riskier.

Decision records usually store the result of a discussion: approved, with conditions. Minutes record consensus because that is what minutes are for. The analyst who argued against it, and the specific risk they named, disappears into the memory of the people who were in the room.

That is a loss twice over.

First, the dissent is frequently where the real falsifier lives. The person who disagreed was usually pointing at the risk that, if anything, would later materialise. When it does, the organisation discovers it was warned only if someone remembers.

Second, dissent histories are the clearest view you will ever get of who reads a class of situation well. Agreement tells you little about individual judgment. Disagreement that turns out right tells you a lot.

## Why groups lose the minority view

The mechanism is well studied. Garold Stasser and William Titus gave members of small groups different information about candidates, arranged so that the best candidate only became visible if members pooled what they privately knew. Their 1985 paper in the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* found groups discussed the information they already shared, usually chose the candidate a plurality favoured at the start, and that discussion "tended to perpetuate, not to correct" the distorted picture. Unshared information that argued against the winner was rarely raised. This design became known as the hidden profile, and it describes most committees: the member with the inconvenient fact is the one least likely to be heard.

Seniority makes it worse. In *Wiser*, Cass Sunstein and Reid Hastie describe groups acting as herds behind their "most senior, most talkative, most authoritative members", and members self-censoring information only they possess. Their advice to leaders is to consider "remaining silent, holding their cards close to their chest" to lower the reputational cost of speaking up.

Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein reach the same conclusion from a different direction. Their "decision hygiene" practices include sequencing information so judges do not leap to conclusions, and "aggregating multiple, independent judgments". Independence is the operative word. Once the room has heard the most senior view, the judgments being aggregated are no longer independent.

| What happens in the room | Research finding | What it does to the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discussion centres on shared facts | Stasser and Titus, 1985 | The fact only the dissenter held never reaches the minutes |
| Members follow the senior voice | Sunstein and Hastie, 2015 | Views captured after discussion are already diluted |
| Independent judgments converge | Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein, 2021 | The aggregate looks like agreement, not evidence |
| Dissent feels risky | Edmondson, 1999 | People stop recording it, or stop holding it |

## How to capture it well

**Independent views first.** Ask each participant to record their view and probability before discussion. Once the most senior person has spoken, views converge, and the dissent you capture afterwards is already diluted.

**One line, attributed, with a probability.** "Against. Customer concentration risk understated; 35% this account is lost within a year." That is enough. The probability makes it scoreable later, using the same method as in [Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/).

**Genuine, not assigned.** A designated devil's advocate produces weaker signal than real disagreement, because everyone knows it is a role. Charlan Nemeth, whose research on dissent spans decades, puts it directly: "devil's advocates don't make you think about the alternative decision." Real conviction is what makes the majority reconsider. Sunstein and Hastie do recommend devil's advocates and red teams as tools for testing a plan, and they have a place. The point is to record assigned challenges separately from genuine dissent, so the two are never mixed when hit rates are calculated.

> Agreement tells you little about individual judgment. Disagreement that turns out right tells you a lot.

## How to use it

At the falsifier check date, review the dissent alongside the outcome. Was the minority right? About the thing they named, or something else?

| Field | Example | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Position | Against | Separating dissent from conditional support |
| Reason | Customer concentration risk understated | Checking whether the named risk occurred |
| Probability | 35% the account is lost within a year | Scoring the dissent against the outcome |
| Type | Genuine or assigned | Keeping devil's advocacy out of hit rates |
| Owner | The person who held the view | Building each person's record by decision class |
| Check date | The decision's falsifier date | Triggering the review |

Over several cycles, track each person's dissent hit rate by decision class. After a while you can weight a dissent from someone with a strong record in that class differently from one without. That is the closest thing to institutional wisdom a system can hold: not a rule, but a memory of whose doubts deserve attention. These fields sit naturally in a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/), and they are the same discipline a [win-loss programme](https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/) applies to deals: compare what people believed with what happened.

## Protecting dissenters

A visible record of who predicted what can feel like exposure, and in some cultures it will suppress candour rather than encourage it. Amy Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company defined team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking", and found it associated with learning behaviour, which in turn related to performance. A dissent record that punishes the people who disagree will destroy the very behaviour it is trying to capture.

So decide deliberately who can see dissent: the panel, the function head, or only the review gate. Do not use dissent records in performance evaluation in the first year. Show people their own hit rate privately before anyone else sees it. The aim is to make disagreement safer, not riskier.

## What would prove this wrong

Recorded dissent proving no more predictive of bad outcomes than majority views over a meaningful number of decisions. Then dissent is noise, and the record is clutter. The group research shows why minority information gets lost; it does not prove that the minority is usually right, which is why the record needs outcomes, not just positions.

## lowob takeaways

- **Collect views before discussion.** Independence disappears once the senior person speaks.
- **One attributed line with a probability.** Enough to score later, short enough to keep.
- **Separate genuine from assigned.** Devil's advocacy has uses but does not belong in hit rates.
- **Protect the dissenter.** Limited visibility, private feedback, and no performance use in year one.

## Common questions

### Why should committees record dissenting views?

The dissenter is often pointing at the risk that later materialises, and dissent histories show who reads a class of situation well. Research on group discussion shows minority information is otherwise rarely surfaced or kept.

### How do I capture dissent in decision meetings?

Ask each participant to record their view and a probability before discussion, then keep dissent as one attributed line with a probability, separate from assigned challenges, and review it at the decision's check date.

### Does a devil's advocate count as dissent?

Not for scoring. Charlan Nemeth's research finds role-played objections stimulate less reconsideration than genuine dissent. Record assigned challenges separately.

### What is a hidden profile in group decision making?

An experimental setup in which the best option only becomes clear if members pool information they hold privately. Stasser and Titus found groups mostly discussed shared information and missed it.

## Next Move

At the next committee decision, ask every member to write their view and a probability on paper before anyone speaks. Keep any dissent as one attributed line in the record, and diary the date you will check it.
